summary: The two things I was asked to verify by measurement PASS. All three clean-read mutants die (stat -> Optional.empty(), get -> zero-byte stream, list -> empty ListPage), each killed by theCLEANREADSReturnWhatTheDelegateHoldsAndNotAnEmptyView and nothing else. Both accessor mutants die independently (List.copyOf -> Collections.unmodifiableList, and Map.copyOf -> the live map, and Map.copyOf -> Collections.unmodifiableMap), each killed by bothACCESSORSHandBackACOPYAndNotAViewOfTheirLiveState; a genuine copy of a different Map class (new TreeMap<>(drawCounts)) correctly survives, so the test distinguishes copy from view rather than pinning an implementation. drawCounts() -> Map.of() is caught elsewhere (everyClassDrawsOnEVERYFaultingCall...), so the new test is not the only thing holding it. The M4.12 coverage sentence is true in BOTH directions: I re-measured the newly-named positive claims (clean putIfAbsent payload, clean putIfMatch version, put and delete delegation -- all killed) and the negative claims (countDraw label swap SURVIVES, close() no-op SURVIVES, and nothing in any of the three classes calls store.close(), multipart() or capabilities()). Nothing here changes an object-store request rate: it is test-only, and its extra requests scale with faulted calls, not with records, shards, partitions or indices. What is still wrong is entirely in backlog.md. The M4.12 row's WHAT THIS COMMIT CONTAINS sentence -- the sentence written specifically so the row cannot describe a commit other than itself -- names two test classes while three are staged. And the duplicated clauses I raised as Y2 are NOT fixed: both M4.19 and M4.20 still repeat a clause verbatim.

findings.title: The M4.12 row's inventory of the commit names TWO test classes; THREE are staged. FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest appears nowhere in the row.
findings.detail: The row says: '⚠️ WHAT THIS COMMIT CONTAINS, stated because an earlier draft of this row described a commit other than itself: the decorator plus `FaultInjectingStoreTest` (what a fault DOES to a caller) and `FaultInjectingStoreStreamsTest` (WHICH stream a class draws from, and WHEN).' The staged set is FaultInjectingStore.java, FaultInjectingStoreTest.java, FaultInjectingStoreStreamsTest.java AND FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest.java (175 lines, 4 tests). The third file is the one this round exists to deliver -- it holds theCLEANREADSReturnWhatTheDelegateHoldsAndNotAnEmptyView and bothACCESSORSHandBackACOPYAndNotAViewOfTheirLiveState, the two tests that close the round-9 major and my Y1 -- and the row does not name it or say what its seam is. The row's own coverage sentence DOES list the properties (the clean read verbs' RETURNS, the snapshot semantics of BOTH accessors), so the row knows the work happened; only the file inventory is stale. This is the same defect class raised as major two rounds ago at hash 43185b5d8a07, and the sentence that was added to fix it is the sentence that is now wrong -- the split created a third file and the enumeration was not extended. The mirror-image error is inside the tree too: FaultInjectingStoreStreamsTest.java:21 says it was split out 'at 548 lines' and FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest.java:20 says 'SPLIT OUT AT 524 LINES', so the tree records two splits while the authoritative row records one.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.15 is M4's milestone review, and milestone-review/SKILL.md reads backlog.md, which AGENTS.md calls authoritative. A reviewer reconciling the M4.12 row against the tree finds a fourth staged Java file the row does not account for. Two readings are available and both are wrong: that FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest was smuggled in as silent scope widening (AGENTS.md 'Never widen scope silently'), or that it belongs to M4.19/M4.20 like the five untracked files -- in which case it would be deleted or moved and the three clean-read properties plus both accessor-snapshot properties, the exact findings rounds 9 and 10 exist to close, silently leave the tree with the suite still green (I measured that: with the file removed, all six mutants above survive). The fix is one clause naming the file and its seam.
findings.suggestion: Extend the WHAT THIS COMMIT CONTAINS sentence to name FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest and its seam -- the CLEAN non-faulting returns and accessor snapshot semantics -- and reconcile the split count with the two class javadocs (548 then 524), or drop those two line counts, which the row's own 'NO COUNT HERE, deliberately' argument already says go stale.

findings.title: Y2 is NOT fixed: both new rows still carry a verbatim duplicated clause, and M4.20 also carries a severed sentence.
findings.detail: Measured by scanning each row for repeated substrings. M4.19 (line 266): 'Delivers I1-I5 as predicates over the raw objects, I1-I5 as predicates over the raw objects.' -- the clause appears twice, separated by a comma. M4.20 (line 267): '... many logical pods, one seed, driven through the `Sequencer` seam, with failover BOTH ways -- a polite release and a TTL lapse -- and fenced leaders that do not know it yet -- many logical pods, one seed, through the `Sequencer` seam, with failover both ways (a polite release and a TTL lapse) and fenced leaders that do not know it yet.' -- the whole acceptance-criteria clause is stated twice, once with em-dashes and once with parentheses. Separately, M4.20 has a severed sentence: '⚠️ Also `withZone` returns `this`, violating the `Clock` contract -- ⚠️ NEITHER `CommitProtocolSimulation` NOR `SimulatedClock` IS TRACKED YET' -- the withZone clause's consequence is missing and the trailing '--' runs straight into the next warning. M4.20 also closes with a bare '⚠️ SPLIT OUT OF M4.12.' that duplicates its own opening '`SimulatedClock` MOVED HERE FROM M4.12'.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.19 and M4.20 are rows nobody has worked yet; the next hand reads them cold. A duplicated acceptance-criteria clause in two slightly different wordings reads as two requirements -- 'driven through the Sequencer seam' and 'through the Sequencer seam' -- and the second, parenthesised copy is the one a reader stops at, so the em-dash copy's 'BOTH ways' emphasis is lost. The severed withZone sentence names a Clock-contract violation and then does not say what to do about it, so the M4.20 worker either re-derives it or drops it. Minor, so it lands on a pass; recorded because it was raised at 43185b5d8a07 and again at f7dbfa87d6cf and is still measurably present at 655d658cc06f.
findings.suggestion: Delete the second copy of each clause. Complete or delete the withZone sentence. Delete the trailing 'SPLIT OUT OF M4.12.' in M4.20.

findings.title: The ambiguousPut fault can only ever resolve as LANDED on a write that would have won, and the row's WHAT IS NOT MODELLED list does not disclose it -- while AmbiguousPutStore.Mode.LOST in the same package models exactly the case the injector cannot reach.
findings.detail: Both ambiguous arms (putIfAbsent at :203-216, putIfMatch at :273-279) attempt the delegate write and then throw. There is no path where the fault fires and the write is WITHHELD. So whenever the conditional write would have succeeded -- a free key, or a matching Version -- the injected ambiguity always resolves to 'it landed'. The LOST resolution is reachable only incidentally, when the CAS would have failed anyway (anAmbiguousPutIfAbsentSTILLLOSESToAnOccupiedSlot, anAmbiguousPutIfMatchSTILLLOSESToASTALEVersion). The sibling double AmbiguousPutStore.java:39-45 already has an explicit Mode.LOST -- 'The store never saw it; the version is unchanged' -- and its javadoc argues that distinguishing the two halves 'is the whole task'. The M4.12 row's WHAT IS NOT MODELLED paragraph lists delayed writes, reordered completions and partitioned leaders, and says of ambiguousPut only that it covers BOTH conditional writes, so a reader concludes the class is complete.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13's sweep drives LeaseManager through this decorator. Renew's only CAS is putIfMatch with a version the holder believes current, so under this injector every ambiguous renew LANDS and every retry self-fences -- the dangerous half, which is correctly the one M4.3d/g/h care about. But the benign half never occurs: no seed ever produces 'the renew threw, nothing landed, retry with the SAME version must succeed'. A protocol defect confined to that path -- a needless epoch bump on a retry after a clean-but-ambiguous failure, say, which burns an epoch and so feeds M4.16's unsealed-ancestor I2 violation -- is unreachable by the sweep, and the row tells its reader the ambiguous class is covered on both writes so nobody looks.
findings.suggestion: Either add the gap to the row's WHAT IS NOT MODELLED list next to the putIfMatch/unreachable gap already recorded there, and hand it to M4.13 with the others; or draw a fourth coin for the landed/lost resolution. Cross-referencing AmbiguousPutStore from the class javadoc would also stop the next hand re-deriving which of the two doubles to reach for.

findings.title: The third split's seam does not hold: the new class's javadoc says 'what the injector does when it is NOT injecting', but one of its four tests fires a fault on every call, and the accessor-snapshot property is now half in each file with a comment pointing across.
findings.detail: The class javadoc at :17-33 states the seam as the CLEAN paths -- 'the CLEAN paths are a separate concern from the faulting arms' -- yet bothACCESSORSHandBackACOPYAndNotAViewOfTheirLiveState (:145-175) constructs Faults(1.0, 0, 0) and drives two faulting stat() calls; it is not a clean-path test at all. Its comment at :146-149 then names theInjectedRecordIsASNAPSHOTACallerCannotMutate, which lives in the other file at FaultInjectingStoreTest.java:269-280. So the two halves of one property -- 'the accessor is UNMODIFIABLE' and 'the accessor is a COPY' -- are now in two classes, each carrying half the argument, with the newer half explaining why the older half was insufficient. The javadoc's own concession ('plus accessor hygiene') is the tell that the seam was widened to fit rather than chosen.
findings.failure_scenario: The next hand at M4.13 or M4.19 needs to know which class a new test belongs in. A class whose name says Delegation, whose javadoc says NOT injecting, and which contains a p=1.0 fault test answers 'anywhere', so tests land by coin flip and the next 500-line split has no seam to cut on. Concretely: someone tidying the older, weaker theInjectedRecordIsASNAPSHOT... test -- which is now strictly subsumed by the newer one's list assertion -- deletes it from FaultInjectingStoreTest without noticing the surviving comment in the other file still credits it, and the UnsupportedOperationException half of the property goes with it (Collections.unmodifiableList still dies via the size assertion, but a return of `new ArrayList<>(injected)` -- a real copy that is freely mutable by its reader -- would then survive both files).
findings.suggestion: Either move theInjectedRecordIsASNAPSHOTACallerCannotMutate next to bothACCESSORSHandBackACOPY... and rename the class to say what it holds (clean paths AND accessor hygiene), or fold the unmodifiable assertion into the new test and delete the old one. Also FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest.java:175 closes the class as '}}' on the last statement's line, and FaultInjectingStoreTest.java has six multi-line blank runs left by the two extractions (102-105, 176-178, 236-239, 281-284, 315-316, 397-399) -- no formatter gate exists to catch either.

findings.title: The two splits left three copies of body(String) and two of read(MemoryBinStore, String), byte-identical, across the three classes.
findings.detail: body(String) is defined at FaultInjectingStoreTest.java:40, FaultInjectingStoreStreamsTest.java:39 and FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest.java:38. read(MemoryBinStore, String) is defined at FaultInjectingStoreTest.java:171 and FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest.java:43. All copies are identical. The package already has the convention for shared test doubles (AmbiguousPutStore, PutOrderStore, StatBlindStore and five others are top-level classes), so a shared fixture holder is not a new idea here.
findings.failure_scenario: These three classes exist to be compared against each other: FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest establishes the clean baseline and the other two assert what a fault does to it, and its javadoc says so ('the baseline every faulted run is compared against'). If Body gains a required field, or the charset in body() changes, or read() starts asserting something, the change must be made in three places; one missed copy means the baseline class writes different bytes from the faulting classes with every test still green -- which is precisely the 'a decorator that is wrong when it injects NOTHING corrupts the control run' failure the file was added to prevent, arriving through the fixture instead of through the decorator.
findings.suggestion: Hoist body() and read() into one package-private helper in the same package, as the eight existing store doubles already are.

findings.title: Nothing constrains where the request meter sits relative to this decorator, and the wrong order hides the requests the decorator adds.
findings.detail: duplicatePut issues a SECOND delegate.putIfAbsent (:226) and the ambiguousPut arms issue a delegate write and then throw, so the caller's retry adds a third. aDUPLICATEDPutREALLYREACHESTheStoreTwice... (FaultInjectingStoreTest.java:213-214) composes them as FaultInjectingStore(CountingBinStore(MemoryBinStore)) -- meter BELOW the injector -- and measures 2 puts, which is the correct order and the reason that assertion works. Nothing in the decorator's javadoc, in the row, or in any test says the order is load-bearing.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.9 asserts bounded recovery by REQUEST COUNT through CountingBinStore, and its row says so; M4.13 then runs that sweep under injected faults. If a future harness composes CountingBinStore(new FaultInjectingStore(store, seed, faults)) -- the natural reading, meter outermost so it counts 'what the caller asked for' -- every injected duplicate PUT and every ambiguous landing write becomes invisible to the meter. A recovery under faults could then issue twice the conditional writes it is budgeted for and report the budget green, which is a cost threshold passing while the requests happen: exactly the class of blindness cost.md R9 and the counting decorator exist to close.
findings.suggestion: One javadoc line on the class saying the meter belongs BELOW the injector, because the injector's own retries are real requests and must be counted. Cheaper than a gate and it is where the next hand will read it.
